title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: When Levin thought about what he was and what he was living for, he could find no answer to the questions and was reduced to despair — so he stopped asking himself. It was as though he did know what he was and what he was living for, since he acted and lived with resolve and without hesitation. In fact, in those days he was more decisive and surer in life than he had ever been.

When he went back to the country at the beginning of June, he also went back to his usual occupations. Running the estate, his dealings with the peasants and the neighbors, the management of his household, looking after his sister's and brother's properties — which he was in charge of — his relationships with his wife and her family, the care of his child, and the new beekeeping hobby he had picked up that spring all filled up his time.

These things absorbed him now, not because he could justify them to himself by some set of general principles, the way he used to. On the contrary, disillusioned by the failure of his earlier efforts for the common good, and too occupied with his own thoughts and the pile of business pressing on him from every direction, he had given up entirely on thinking about the general welfare. He went about all this work simply because it seemed to him that he had to do it — that he could not do otherwise. In the old days — practically from childhood, and increasingly into full manhood — whenever he had tried to do something that would be good for all, for humanity, for Russia, for the whole village, he had noticed that the idea of it was pleasant, but the work itself was always confused, that he was never fully convinced it was strictly necessary, and that the project, which had begun by looking so grand, would shrink smaller and smaller until it vanished into nothing. But now, since his marriage, when he had begun to confine himself more and more to living for himself, even though he felt no particular pleasure at the thought of the work he was doing, he felt a total conviction that it was necessary, saw that it succeeded far better than in earlier days, and that it kept growing.
Now, almost against his own will, he was cutting deeper and deeper into the soil like a plough, so that he could not be pulled back out without turning the furrow aside.

To live the same kind of family life his father and forefathers had lived — that is, on the same cultural footing — and to bring up his children in the same way, was unquestionably necessary. It was as necessary as eating when you were hungry. And to do that, just as it was necessary to cook a meal, it was necessary to keep the machinery of farming at Pokrovskoe running so that it produced an income. Just as unmistakably as it was necessary to repay a debt, it was necessary to keep the estate in such shape that his son, when he received it, would say "thank you" to his father, the same way Levin had said "thank you" to his grandfather for everything he had built and planted. And to do that, it was necessary to look after the land himself, not lease it out, and to breed cattle, fertilize the fields, and plant trees.

It was impossible not to look after Sergey Ivanovitch's affairs, his sister's, and the peasants' who came to him for advice and were used to doing so — as impossible as dropping a child you're carrying in your arms. It was necessary to see to the comfort of his sister-in-law and her children, and of his wife and the baby, and impossible not to spend at least a small part of each day with them.
All of this, together with shooting and the new beekeeping, filled up the whole of Levin's life — a life that had no meaning at all for him as soon as he began to think.
But besides knowing thoroughly what he had to do, Levin also knew, in just the same way, _how_ he had to do all of it, and which things mattered more than the rest.

He knew he had to hire workers as cheaply as he could, but to hire men under bond — paying them up front at less than the going wage — was something he must not do, however profitable it would have been. Selling straw to the peasants when feed was scarce was something he could do, even though he felt sorry for them; but the tavern and the pothouse had to be shut down, even though they brought in income. Cutting down his timber had to be punished as severely as possible, but he couldn't impose fines on peasants whose cattle wandered into his fields; and though it annoyed the gamekeeper and made the peasants unafraid to graze their cattle on his land, he couldn't impound their animals as a penalty.

He had to lend Pyotr, who was paying a money-lender ten per cent a month, enough to get clear of him. But he couldn't let peasants who didn't pay their rent off the hook, or let them fall into arrears. There was no overlooking the bailiff's failure to mow the meadows and letting the hay rot — and equally, no way to mow the acres where a young copse had been planted. There was no excusing a laborer who had gone home in the busy season because his father was dying, however much sympathy he had for him, and he had to dock those expensive idle months from his pay. But there was no question of refusing the monthly rations to the old servants who weren't fit for anything else.

Levin knew that when he got home he would have to go first to his wife, who wasn't well, and that the peasants who had been waiting three hours to see him could wait a little longer. He also knew that, however much pleasure he got out of taking a swarm, he would have to give up that pleasure and leave the old man to handle the bees alone, while he talked to the peasants who had followed him out to the bee-house.
Whether he was doing the right thing or the wrong thing he did not know, and far from trying to prove that he was right, these days he avoided any thought or talk about it.

Reasoning had led him to doubt, and stopped him from seeing what he ought to do and what he ought not. When he didn't think, but simply lived, he was constantly aware of an infallible judge in his soul deciding which of two possible courses of action was the better and which was the worse, and the moment he didn't act rightly, he knew it.

So he lived, not knowing and not seeing any way of finding out what he was or what he was living for, and tormented by that ignorance to such a degree that he was afraid of suicide — and yet steadily laying down his own particular, definite path in life.
